title: Coniglio in umido
subtitle: Italian braised rabbit with olives, herbs, and white wine
excerpt: Coniglio in umido is a braised rabbit dish from Tuscany and Umbria: rabbit pieces cooked slowly with white wine, olives, herbs, and a little tomato until the meat is tender and the sauce dark. Rabbit benefits from long, gentle cooking; this dish takes about 1 hour from start to finish.
sourceNotes: Central Italian regional recipe. Braised rabbit with olives and wine is a traditional preparation across Tuscany, Umbria, and Lazio. Method drawn from Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina e l'arte di mangiar bene (1891, public domain), and Anna Del Conte, Gastronomy of Italy (2001).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Makes ahead well. Reheat gently over low heat.

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian term for a slow braise in a little liquid, covered: the meat steams in its own moisture alongside the wine and vegetables; the result is tender meat and a concentrated sauce.

content.text: is rabbit braised with olives, rosemary, white wine, and a small amount of tomato. The rabbit pieces brown first to build colour, then braise for 50 minutes until the meat comes cleanly off the bone. The olives and herbs give the sauce its character. Ask the butcher to joint the rabbit if you are not confident with a knife.

items.prepNote: jointed into 8 pieces, about 1.2 kg prepared weight
pitted; Taggiasca or Kalamata work well

content.text: Season {{rabbit}} of rabbit pieces and dust lightly in {{plain-flour}} of flour. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a casserole over medium-high heat. Brown the pieces in batches, 4 minutes per side, until golden. Remove.

In the same pan, cook {{garlic}} of garlic cloves and {{rosemary}} of rosemary sprigs for 2 minutes. Pour in {{dry-white-wine}} of wine and let it reduce by half, scraping up the pan. Add the tomatoes. Return the rabbit. Tuck in the olives.
Cover and braise over medium-low heat for 50 minutes, turning the pieces halfway, until the meat is tender and coming off the bone. Season and serve with polenta, pasta, or bread.

items.cause: Braised at too high a temperature, or not enough liquid.
items.fix: Rabbit dries out quickly. Use a tight-fitting lid and the lowest heat that keeps a bare simmer. Add a splash of water or wine if the pot looks dry.

items.cause: Inferior or very sharp olives used.
items.fix: Use mild, oil-cured olives (Taggiasca) rather than brine-cured. Rinse brine-cured olives thoroughly before adding.

content.text: Rabbit is a farmhouse meat across Tuscany, Umbria, and the hill towns of Lazio. The in umido method (braised in wine and olives) is the most common home approach: once the lid goes on, the rabbit looks after itself. Artusi includes several rabbit braises in his 1891 book, treating it as everyday food rather than a special-occasion ingredient.
